pedagogy.summary: Children find different combinations of coins that make the same total — e.g. 50p as one 50p, or two 20p and a 10p, or five 10p. The valuable skill is doing this SYSTEMATICALLY (starting from the largest coin, or swapping one coin for equivalent smaller ones) rather than at random, and understanding that the sets are equal because their VALUES sum to the same total even though the coins differ. A key constraint: only real denominations exist — there is no 8p coin, but any total can be built from the coins that do exist.
bestPractices: Work with real coins; build one total several different ways
Model a systematic method: start with the largest coin, or swap a coin for equivalent smaller ones (50p to two 20p + 10p)
Ask 'can you find another way?' and record each combination in an organised list
Discuss why the sets are equal — the same total value, different coins
Reinforce that only real denominations exist (no 8p coin), but any total can be made from them
keyRepresentations: Real coins arranged into equal-value sets
A part-whole model (total = these coins / those coins)
An organised list or table of combinations
Swapping one coin for equivalent smaller coins
commonMisconceptions: Uses a non-existent coin (e.g. an '8p') to make a total
Finds combinations unsystematically, repeating some and missing others
Tracks the number of coins rather than their total value
Thinks a set with more coins must be worth more, so two ways can't be equal

learn.summary: Year 2 learners (ages 6-7) find different combinations of real coins that make the same total (e.g. 50p as one 50p, or two 20p + a 10p, or five 10p). The core skill is working SYSTEMATICALLY — starting from the largest coin, or swapping one coin for equivalent smaller ones — and understanding that different coin sets are equal because their VALUES sum to the same total, even though the coins differ. A key constraint: only real denominations exist (there is no 8p coin), but any total can be built from the coins that do exist.

activities.title: Build a target several ways with a live-updating total
feedback: If a learner grabs for a coin that doesn't exist (e.g. an '8p'), note that there is no such coin and ask which real coins could make that part of the total instead.

When a learner finds a new combination, ask 'Can you find another way?' and add it to the organised list. Only ask 'How could you be SURE you've found them all?' when the coins allowed are limited (e.g. only 10p, 20p and 50p for 50p), because with every coin from 1p upwards there are hundreds of ways to make 50p.
If two valid ways look very different, pause on the moment the totals match: 'This set looks completely different but is worth exactly the same — why?'
activities.rationale: The National Curriculum requires Year 2 pupils to find different combinations of coins equal to the same amount. A live total and an organised record support the equal-value idea and encourage systematic enumeration. A live-updating total and an organised board are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not a required product; the same work can be done with real coins by hand.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'find different combinations of coins that equal the same amounts of money'.
White Rose Y2 Money teaches making the same amount in different ways using part-whole models, and documents pupils counting the number of coins rather than their value.
learnerActions: Take a target amount (e.g. 50p) and drag or place real-denomination coins into a tray until they reach the total.
Watch a running total so you can see when the tray reaches exactly 50p.
Once a valid way is found, record it on an organised board or list of 'ways to make 50p', then find another distinct way.
Work from the largest coin first, or swap a coin for equivalent smaller ones, so the search is organised rather than random.
Only real coins are available on the shelf (no 8p), so every solution is one that could really be paid.
activities.intendedInsight: Many different coin sets can share the same total value; building each one and watching the total confirm the target makes 'equal value, different coins' directly visible.

activities.title: Swap a coin for equivalent smaller coins without changing the total
feedback: If a learner thinks the five-10p set is 'more' than a single 50p because it has more coins, count the VALUE of each set to the same total and show that more coins can equal fewer coins in value.
Prompt: 'You made 30p with three 10p. Can you make 30p using a 20p? What else do you need?' to rehearse swap reasoning.
Reinforce that the swap did not change the amount, only the coins used.
activities.rationale: Swapping directly targets the misconception that more coins means more money, and models a systematic route between combinations. A live swap action is an optional interaction example; the same reasoning can be done with real coins by hand.
sourceClaims: NCETM guidance notes that a mathematically correct total may use a non-existent coin, and cautions: 'For example, we do not have an 8p coin, but any value can be made of existing denominations of coins'; it also directs attention to making an amount 'in the fewest number of coins', focusing on value rather than count.
White Rose Y2 Money teaches making the same amount in different ways using part-whole models, and documents pupils counting the number of coins rather than their value.
learnerActions: Start with one way of making the total (e.g. a single 50p).
Swap one coin for equivalent smaller coins — lift the 50p and replace it with two 20p and a 10p — and check the total is unchanged.
Try other swaps (e.g. 30p made as three 10p; swap to 20p + 10p) and confirm each keeps the same value.
Describe in words why the new set equals the old one: the coin values still sum to the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Exchanging one coin for equivalent smaller coins keeps the total fixed, so a set with more coins can be worth exactly the same as a set with fewer coins.

activities.title: Sort and match coin sets to totals (recognition practice)
feedback: If a learner accepts a set that relies on a non-existent 8p coin, point out there is no 8p coin and ask which real coins could make that value.
If a set is wrongly rejected, re-count its value to the total together.
activities.rationale: Recognition tasks give quick practice judging totals and catching the invented-coin error. As noted in the constraints, selecting from given sets checks judgement of value but does not itself require the learner to construct combinations, so it should accompany building tasks, not replace them.
sourceClaims: NCETM guidance notes that a mathematically correct total may use a non-existent coin, and cautions: 'For example, we do not have an 8p coin, but any value can be made of existing denominations of coins'; it also directs attention to making an amount 'in the fewest number of coins', focusing on value rather than count.
learnerActions: Decide which of several coin sets make a given total (e.g. 'which of these make 50p?').
Sort sets into 'makes 50p' and 'does not make 50p'.
Match a total to a valid coin set.
Spot and reject any set that relies on a non-existent coin, such as an invented 8p.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking whether a coin set reaches a stated total, and rejecting sets that use invented coins, reinforces that value is what matters and that only real denominations may be used.

activities.title: Pay a different way — shopkeeper talk (optional spoken extension)
feedback: If the learner stops after one way, prompt 'Is there another way to make 50p?' and keep a shared list of ways found.
Ask 'Could you make 50p with an 8p coin? Why not?' to surface the real-denominations constraint.
activities.rationale: A spoken prompt can elicit further combinations and their justification. It is best paired with real coins or an organised record, because a spoken exchange alone does not display systematic enumeration as clearly.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'find different combinations of coins that equal the same amounts of money'.
learnerActions: Respond to a shopkeeper asking 'Can you pay 50p a different way?' by naming or laying out another valid coin set.
Explain aloud why the new way is worth the same as the first.
Be challenged to find yet another way, and, when only a few coin types are allowed (e.g. 10p, 20p and 50p), to say how you could be sure you've found them all.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining and justifying equal-value combinations aloud rehearses the reasoning and the language of 'same total, different coins'.

constraints: Use only real coin denominations; there is no 8p (or 3p) coin, though any total can be built from the coins that do exist.

Systematic enumeration develops with age and practice: treat random searching not as an error to punish but as a cue to model one system (largest coin first, then swap down) and record each way on an organised list.
Recognition and sorting tasks (choosing which given sets make a total) check judgement of value but do not require independent construction of combinations; include building tasks for production.
A static 'ways to make 50p' poster can display combinations but does not let the learner build or swap them; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main activity.

Assess by watching HOW combinations are generated (systematic vs random, real coins vs an invented coin) and by asking why two different sets are equal — this distinguishes secure combining from guesswork and catches the more-coins-means-more-money misconception.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing' and framed the quiz as merely scoring; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened or dropped. The source claims do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium.
The White Rose source (part-whole models; coin-counting misconception) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specifics as unconfirmed.

Interaction examples (live total, drag coins, swap tool, organised board) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and optional, not mandatory implementation details. An earlier draft mentioned a 'recolour' action not in the original design notes; it has been removed.

probeDeeper: 'Is there another way to make 50p? How could you be SURE you've found them all?'
'These two piles look different — one has more coins. Are they really the same amount? How do you know?'
'Could you make 50p with an 8p coin? Why not?'
'You made 30p with three 10p. Can you make 30p using a 20p? What else do you need?' (swap reasoning)
assess.correctAnswer: Produces several valid combinations for 50p (e.g. 50p; 20p + 20p + 10p; five 10p) using only real coins; works with some system (largest-first or swapping) rather than at random; explains the sets are equal because their values total the same 50p.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a non-existent coin (e.g. an '8p' or '3p') to make a total
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep only real coins available; check each combination is payable with actual denominations, noting that any total can still be made from the coins that exist.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds a total using a coin that doesn't exist as a real denomination

errorPatterns.pattern: Works unsystematically — repeats a combination or gives up after one, with no order to the search
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat random searching as an error to correct — systematic enumeration develops with age and practice. Instead, model one system (start from the largest coin, then swap down) and record each way on an organised list so the child sees the pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Repeats the same combination, or stops after one way, with no system

errorPatterns.pattern: Tracks the number of coins rather than total value — thinks a set with more coins is worth more, so two ways can't be equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the VALUE of each set to the same total; show that more coins can equal fewer coins in value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the five-10p set is 'more' than the single 50p because it has more coins

responseLevels.gap: Uses invented coins or repeats one combination; judges sets by number of coins.
responseLevels.full: Systematically finds multiple valid combinations for a total using real denominations, and explains they are equal because the coin values sum to the same amount.
responseLevels.partial: Finds two or three valid combinations with real coins, but searches at random and can't be sure they are all found, or is unsure why the sets are equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set a make-the-total task and WATCH how the child works: (1) 'Show me 50p using these coins. Now make 50p a DIFFERENT way. And another way.' (2) Watch whether they work systematically (largest coin first, or swapping) or at random. (3) 'You made 50p with a 50p coin, and with two 20p and a 10p — why are they the same amount?' Watch for use of real denominations only, an organised approach, and whether they track value.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW they generate combinations (systematic vs random, real coins vs an invented 8p) separates secure combining from guesswork; asking why two sets are equal catches a child who thinks more coins must mean more money.
